title: Guessing and regret
cando: talk about imaginary situations, guess what happened and talk about regrets

about.text: In this lesson, something goes wrong at work, and people try to work out why. You guess what happened with must have and might have, talk about regrets with should have, and talk about things that are not true with if and I wish. You also read a fair account of a problem, and write one of your own.
goals: Guess the cause of a problem: It must have been… It can't have been…
Talk about regrets: I should have double-checked it.
Talk about things that are not true now: If I had more time, I'd… I wish I knew…
Give advice with If I were you, I'd…
Write six wishes and a fair account of what went wrong.

chapters.title: Everything looks obvious afterwards
chapters.text:
This lesson is about things that go wrong, and how we talk about them.
When something goes wrong, we look for clues. Then we guess what happened.
In the conversation, Mei and Kwame find the café's freezer switched off. All the food in it is soft. The plug is on the floor.
Mei says: It must have been the new cleaner. Kwame says: Let's not blame anyone yet.
Listen for three phrases. It must have been… If I were you… I should have…
Listen to how quickly people say them. Should have sounds like should-uv. Must have sounds like must-uv. But when you write, always write have.

chapters.title: Guesses, regrets and wishes
chapters.text:
There are two grammar points.
The first is about things that are not true now. If I had more time, I'd check everything twice. But I don't have more time. The verb is past, but the meaning is now.
To give advice, say: If I were you, I'd ring them today.
To say you want something to be different, use I wish and a past verb. I wish I knew what happened. I don't know.
The second point is about guessing the past. Must have means you are almost sure. It must have been the cleaners. Can't have means you are almost sure it didn't happen. Might have means perhaps.
Should have is for regrets. I should have checked it. I didn't check it, and that was a mistake.

chapters.title: A fair account
chapters.text:
In Section 3 you read a short review. Kwame, the kitchen manager, explains what went wrong with the freezer.
He doesn't point the finger at one person. He finds a series of small problems: a lack of communication, no written procedure, and an alarm that wasn't working properly.
That is a fair account. It explains what happened, without blaming people unfairly.
Then you write two things. First, six wishes about your own life. Then a short, fair account of something that went wrong.

chapters.title: Talking it through
chapters.text:
In the real-life task, you talk to a friend about something that went wrong for you.
Say what happened. Then say the likely cause. It must have happened at security.
Say what you should have done. I should have checked the gate earlier.
Last, say what you would do differently. If it happened again, I'd go straight to the gate.
Be honest, but be fair to yourself too. Everybody makes mistakes.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer story or article in which something goes wrong.
As you read, look for the clues. Can you work out what happened before the end?
Then answer the questions, and say what the people should have done.

warmup.prompt: Something has gone wrong at work, and nobody knows why. What do you do first?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. It usually helps to find out the facts before you decide who or what is to blame.

conversation.title: Everything looks obvious afterwards
conversation.setting: It's Monday morning at the Copper Pot Café. Mei, the cook, has just found the big freezer switched off. Kwame, the kitchen manager, comes to look.
lines: Mei
Kwame, come and look at this. The freezer's off, and everything in it is soft.
Kwame
Oh no. That's hundreds of pounds of food. What went wrong?
Mei
Here's a clue: the plug is on the floor. Somebody must have pulled it out.
Kwame
Well, it can't have fallen out by itself. Who was here last?
Mei
The cleaners came in last night. It must have been the new one. I suspect she needed the socket for the floor machine.
Kwame
Maybe, but let's not assume anything, and let's not blame anyone yet. Nobody did this on purpose.
Mei
I know. But I feel so guilty. I was the last one out on Saturday. I should have double-checked it.
Kwame
You've got nothing to be ashamed of. It was working fine when you left.
Mei
Then why didn't the alarm go off? I wish I knew. There must be an explanation.
Kwame
The battery might be flat. I'll ring the cleaning company and try to work out what happened.
Mei
If I were you, I'd put a sign on that plug today.
Kwame
Good idea. Everything looks obvious afterwards, doesn't it? We should have had a sign there from the start.
Mei
Well, we've learned our lesson. Now, how do we put this right before lunch?

questions.a: The plug is on the floor.
questions.why: Mei says: Here's a clue: the plug is on the floor.

questions.a: She was the last one out on Saturday.
wrong: She forgot to call the cleaners.
questions.why: Mei says she was the last one out on Saturday and should have double-checked it.

questions.q: What does Mei advise Kwame to do?
questions.a: put a sign on the plug
questions.why: She says: If I were you, I'd put a sign on that plug today.

phrases.use: Asking about the cause of a problem.

phrases.text: It must have been the new one.
phrases.use: Saying what you are almost sure happened.

phrases.text: It can't have fallen out by itself.
phrases.use: Saying what you are almost sure did not happen.
Stopping people from blaming before the facts are clear.
Saying you are sorry you did not do something.
Saying you want to know something, but you don't.

phrases.text: If I were you, I'd put a sign on that plug.
How do we put this right?
phrases.use: Moving from the problem to a solution.

items.meaning: To stop working well, or to happen in a way that was not planned.
items.example: Everything went wrong on my first day: I was late, and I lost my pass.

items.meaning: To find the answer to something by thinking about it carefully.
items.example: We still can't work out why the machine stopped.

items.meaning: A small fact that helps you find the answer to a problem.
items.example: The wet floor was the first clue that the pipe was leaking.

items.meaning: A reason that makes something easy to understand.
items.example: The bank gave me no explanation for the extra charge.

items.meaning: To think that something is probably true, often something bad, without being sure.
items.example: I suspect the parcel went to the wrong flat.

items.meaning: To think that something is true without checking it.
items.example: I assumed the meeting was at ten, but it was at nine.

items.meaning: To say that somebody or something caused a problem.
items.example: Don't blame the driver. The road was closed.

items.meaning: Because you wanted to, not by accident.
items.example: I'm sure he didn't break it on purpose.

items.meaning: To watch, listen or think carefully about something.
items.example: Please pay attention to the safety instructions.

items.meaning: To check something again, to be completely sure.
items.example: Always double-check the address before you send an email.

items.meaning: In another way.
items.example: If I did the course again, I'd study differently.

items.meaning: Feeling bad about something you did, because you know it was wrong.
items.example: I was ashamed of the way I spoke to him.

items.meaning: Feeling bad because you did something wrong, or did not do something you should.
items.example: I feel guilty that I forgot my sister's birthday.

items.meaning: To understand, after a bad experience, what not to do again.
items.example: I lost my phone twice. Now I've learned my lesson, and I keep it in my bag.

items.meaning: To correct a mistake or repair a problem.
items.example: The bank made a mistake, but they put it right the same day.

sound.title: should've and must've
sound.explain: In fast speech, have is short and weak. Should have sounds like should-uv, and must have sounds like must-uv. I would becomes I'd. When you write, always write have, never of. Listen, then say each group.
lines: I should have double-checked it.
It must have been the new one.
If I were you, I'd put a sign on that plug.

sayIt.instructions: Say Mei's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Do should have and must have sound short and quick?
lines: Here's a clue: the plug is on the floor. Somebody must have pulled it out.
I know. But I feel so guilty. I was the last one out on Saturday. I should have double-checked it.
Then why didn't the alarm go off? I wish I knew. There must be an explanation.
If I were you, I'd put a sign on that plug today.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Two are guesses about the past. One is a regret. Two are about things that are not true.
examples: It must have been the new one.
It can't have fallen out by itself.
If I were you, I'd put a sign on that plug today.
spot.question: Which sentence means: I'm almost sure it happened? I'm almost sure it didn't happen? I didn't do it, and that was a mistake? Which two talk about something that is not true?
spot.answer: must have: almost sure it happened. can't have: almost sure it didn't happen. should have: Mei didn't check, and she thinks she should have. I wish I knew and If I were you are not true: Mei doesn't know, and she isn't Kwame.

rules.title: If I had…, I would… and I wish
rule: If + past, would + verb: a situation that is not true now.
If I had more time, I'd check it every night. (I don't have more time.)
Advice: If I were you, I'd ring them today.
I wish + past or could, about now: I wish I knew. I wish I could help.
I wish + would, about other people: I wish they would reply.
rules.mistake: Never put would after if. Not: If I would have time, I'd help. Say: If I had time, I'd help.

rules.title: must have, might have, should have
rule: must have + past participle: I'm almost sure. It must have been the cleaners.
might have or could have: perhaps. The battery might have died.
can't have: I'm almost sure it didn't happen. It can't have been Omar. He was away.
should have: I didn't do it, and that was a mistake. I should have checked it.
shouldn't have: I did it, and that was a mistake. I shouldn't have left early.
rules.mistake: Write have, not of. It sounds like should-uv, but you write: I should have checked it.

practice.q: If I ___ more time, I would check everything twice.
practice.why: If + past simple is for a situation that is not true now.

practice.q: What ___ you do if you found a mistake in your pay?
practice.why: An imagined situation takes would: What would you do if…?

practice.q: I wish I ___ what happened. Nobody will tell me.
practice.why: I wish + past simple is about now: I wish I knew.

practice.q: I wish I ___ help you, but I'm working all weekend.
practice.why: I wish + could is about something you can't do.

practice.q: The door is wide open, and the lock is broken. Somebody ___ got in.
practice.why: The evidence makes you almost sure, so must have.

practice.q: It ___ been Omar. He was on holiday that week.
practice.why: You are almost sure it did not happen, so can't have.

practice.q: I'm not sure why the parcel is late. The driver ___ got lost.
practice.why: You are not sure, so might have: perhaps it happened.

practice.q: I sent the email to the wrong person. I should ___ double-checked the address.
practice.why: should have + past participle; of is only how it sounds.

practice.q: I feel terrible. I ___ shouted at my colleague yesterday.
practice.why: It happened, and it was a mistake, so shouldn't have.

practice.q: If I ___ you, I'd talk to the manager before Friday.
practice.why: Advice uses were: If I were you.

yourTurn.prompt: Your friend says: “I sent a message complaining about my manager to the whole team by mistake! I meant to send it to my sister.” Give your friend advice with If I were you, and say what they should or shouldn't have done.
yourTurn.model: Oh no! If I were you, I'd go and see your manager today and say sorry, before she hears about it from someone else. You shouldn't have written it at work, and you should have double-checked who it was going to. But everybody makes mistakes. I wish I could help more!

text.title: What went wrong on Sunday night
text.body:
WHAT WENT WRONG ON SUNDAY NIGHT
A short review by Kwame Mensah, kitchen manager, Copper Pot Café
On Monday morning we found the big freezer switched off. We lost about £900 of food, and we had to close for lunch.
What happened
The cleaners came in on Sunday evening, as usual. One of them was new. She unplugged the freezer to use the floor machine, because nobody had told her not to. At the end of a long shift she was exhausted, and she forgot to plug it back in.
Why it happened
This was not one person's mistake. It was a series of small problems.
• There was no written procedure for the cleaners.
• There was a lack of communication between our kitchen team and the cleaning company.
• The freezer alarm was not working properly. Its battery was flat, and nobody had checked it.
My conclusion
It would be easy to point the finger at the new cleaner, but that would not be fair. Nobody did anything on purpose. It is easy to judge people afterwards, when everything looks obvious.
In future
1. There will be a sign on the freezer plug: DO NOT UNPLUG.
2. The last person to leave will check the freezer and write the temperature in the book.
3. We will test the alarm every month.
4. I will send the cleaning company a short written procedure this week.

gist.a: A series of small problems caused it, not one person.
wrong: The new cleaner broke the freezer on purpose.
The freezer was old and needs to be replaced.
gist.why: Kwame says it was not one person's mistake, but a series of small problems.

gist.q: What did the problem cost the café?
gist.a: about £900 of food, and they had to close for lunch
wrong: a new freezer and a new cleaner
gist.why: They lost about £900 of food and had to close for lunch.

detail.q: Why did the cleaner unplug the freezer?
wrong: because it was making a noise
detail.why: She unplugged the freezer to use the floor machine.
Its battery was flat, and nobody had checked it.

detail.q: What does Kwame think about blaming the new cleaner?
wrong: It is the right thing to do.
detail.why: He says it would be easy to point the finger at her, but it would not be fair.

detail.q: Who will check the freezer at night in future?
detail.why: The last person to leave will check the freezer and write the temperature in the book.

items.meaning: What you decide is true after you think about all the facts.
items.example: My conclusion is that we need a clearer system.

items.meaning: The correct way of doing something, often written down in steps.
items.example: Follow the fire procedure and leave by the back stairs.

items.meaning: A situation where there is not enough of something, or none at all.
items.example: The project failed because of a lack of money.

items.meaning: Several things of the same kind that happen one after another.
items.example: A series of small delays made us an hour late.

items.meaning: Sharing information between people, by talking, writing or sending messages.
items.example: Good communication between the two shifts is important.

items.meaning: In the correct way, or as well as it should be.
items.example: The window wasn't closed properly, so the rain came in.

items.meaning: Extremely tired.
items.example: I was exhausted after a twelve-hour shift.

items.meaning: To form an opinion about somebody, often too quickly.
items.example: Don't judge her until you know the whole story.

items.meaning: To say that somebody is to blame for something.
items.example: When things go wrong, it's easy to point the finger at the new person.

items.meaning: From now on.
items.example: In future, please lock the door when you leave.

model.title: Six wishes and a fair account
model.body:
Six wishes
I wish I had more time for my family.
I wish I could drive.
I wish my flat had a garden.
I wish I didn't have to work on Saturdays.
I wish I knew more people in my town.
I wish the buses would come on time.
A fair account: the wrong price list
What happened: Last month I sent a client an old price list, and we lost the order.
Why: The new prices were in a different folder, and nobody had told me. There was a lack of communication in the team, and there was no procedure for old files. I was also exhausted after a long week.
My conclusion: I should have double-checked the date on the file. But the old file shouldn't have been in the shared folder either.
In future: We will delete old price lists, and I will always check the date before I send a price.

write.task: First, write six wishes about your life now: your work, your home or your studies. Use three patterns: I wish I had, I wish I could, and I wish somebody would. Then write a short, fair account of something that went wrong, real or made up. Use the headings in the model: What happened, Why, My conclusion, In future.
checklist: I wrote six wishes, with a past verb, could or would after I wish.
My account says what happened and why, without pointing the finger.
I used should have or shouldn't have at least once.
I said what will be different in future.

card.title: What went wrong?
card.situation: Last week something went wrong for you: at work, at home or on a journey. For example, you missed a flight, a parcel went to the wrong address, or you lost an important file.
card.goal: Talk it through with a friend. Say what probably caused it, what you should have done, and what you would do differently next time.

phrases: I'm still trying to work out what went wrong.
It might have been …, but I'm not sure.
prepare.notes: Choose your story, real or made up. Write three notes: the clue that shows the likely cause, what you should have done, and what you would do differently.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, tell your story to a partner. Your partner asks questions and gives you advice with If I were you. Then change roles.
doIt.wehel: You are my friend. Something went wrong for me last week, and I want to talk about it. Ask me what happened and what I think caused it. Then ask me what I would do differently. Give me one piece of advice with If I were you. Use clear, simple English.

model.title: The missed flight
lines: Friend
You look upset. What's wrong?
You
I missed my flight to Lisbon on Saturday. I'm still trying to work out what went wrong.
Friend
Oh no. Were you late?
You
No, I got to the airport two hours early. But when I got to the gate, it was closed.
Friend
Two hours early? Then something must have held you up inside the airport.
You
Yes, the queue at security was enormous. It must have taken over an hour.
Friend
That's bad luck. But didn't you see the screens?
You
No. I was reading on my phone, and I wasn't paying attention. I should have checked the gate earlier.
Friend
Don't feel too guilty. It could happen to anyone. What would you do differently next time?
You
If it happened again, I'd go straight to the gate after security, and read there.
Friend
And if I were you, I'd get the airline's app. It tells you when the gate opens.
You
Good idea. I've definitely learned my lesson!
compare: Did you say what went wrong, and the likely cause with must have or might have?
Did you say what you should have done?
Did you say what you would do differently: If it happened again, I'd…?
Were you fair, to yourself and to other people?

canDo: I can guess what probably happened with must have, might have and can't have.
I can talk about regrets with should have and shouldn't have.
I can talk about things that are not true with If I had…, I'd… and I wish.
I can give advice with If I were you, I'd…
I can write a fair account of what went wrong, without pointing the finger.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. What do you think goes wrong?
reading.talk: What went wrong in the story, and whose fault was it? What should the people have done? Write three or four sentences, or tell Wehel.

quiz.q: If I ___ closer to work, I'd walk every day.
quiz.why: If + past simple is for a situation that is not true now.

quiz.q: The lights are off, and nobody answers the door. They ___ gone out.
quiz.why: The evidence makes you almost sure, so must have.

quiz.q: It ___ been Priya. She was in Spain all week.
quiz.why: You are almost sure it did not happen, so can't have.

quiz.q: I missed the train. I ___ left home earlier.
quiz.why: should have means it didn't happen, and that was a mistake.

quiz.q: I wish I ___ speak Spanish. Our new client is from Madrid.
quiz.why: I wish + could is about an ability you don't have.

quiz.q: He didn't break it ___ purpose. It was an accident.
quiz.why: on purpose means because you wanted to.

quiz.q: When something goes wrong, it's easy to ___ the finger at the new person.
quiz.why: point the finger means say that somebody is to blame.

quiz.q: I'll call you as soon as I ___ home.
quiz.why: After as soon as, use the present simple for the future.

quiz.q: I see your point. ___ , I'm not sure it will work.
quiz.why: However starts a new sentence and shows a contrast.

quiz.q: Please remember ___ the report by Friday.
quiz.why: remember + to is for something that is still to come.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the freezer conversation in pairs. Then describe a new problem, like a flooded kitchen or a lost parcel, and learners guess the cause with must have, might have and can't have.

Day 2: wishes and advice. Each learner says two wishes about their life now, and a partner gives advice with If I were you. Then practise should have and shouldn't have with short stories of mistakes.
Day 3: the real-life task. Learners talk through something that went wrong: the likely cause, what they should have done and what they would do differently. You are the friend who asks questions.
Day 4: talk about the book: what went wrong in it, and whose fault it was. Then two learners read their fair accounts, and the class checks that nobody points the finger unfairly.
